title: Why I Would Love If My Children Became Teachers
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by meeting a mother and daughter teaching in the same district, Stuart answers the increasingly common line that nobody should be advised to enter teaching today. He concedes the profession is in dark times for many teachers, then gives three reasons he would be delighted if his daughters chose it. The first is that teaching is a noble vocation, noble because the hours are spent serving students' long-term flourishing and a vocation because the word means a calling rather than a way of paying bills; he stresses that this reason, unlike the others, can never be altered by scandal or policy. The second is that teaching remains a viable living, provided one practises contentment, lives near where one teaches and buys less house than one can afford, since joy and meaning are inside jobs rather than products of circumstance. The third is that teaching is still friendly to avocations, which he illustrates with the writing life he imagined as an undergraduate and eventually found through this blog. The piece closes with the prediction that parents and educators will not tolerate teacher shortages and testing gluts indefinitely, so conditions will improve before his own daughters reach college age.
points: Stuart separates the one permanent reason to enter teaching, the nobility of the vocation, from the contingent ones that policy and pay can spoil.
He argues that the financial case for teaching survives if contentment and restraint are treated as skills, naming concrete trade-offs such as housing, cars and where you live.
The claim that joy and meaning are inside jobs is used against the modern expectation that one can micro-design the circumstances of a life.
Avocational room is presented as a genuine feature of the job, evidenced by his own writing career emerging slowly out of teaching summers.
The piece answers the widespread advice never to recommend teaching by predicting that parents and educators will force conditions to improve rather than tolerate shortages and testing gluts.
quotes: During a speaking engagement in New York several weeks ago, I met a mother and a daughter who both teach in the district I was working with. I had goosebumps while I was talking with them — two generations of the same household, enthusiastically serving in the same district.

Noble because it is a beautiful, admirable thing to expend one's working hours in the service of the long-term flourishing of one's students. I think there's a special nobility in nearly any kind of work, but I, from an admittedly biased standpoint, find that to be especially true about teaching.

Vocation because that word used to, and still does, mean something more than how you pay your bills. Teaching as a calling ( vocar = “to call” in Latin, says my Google etymology search ) is something different from how much money one makes or how much prestige the public attaches to your job. It would be a great delight to find that, in any of my children, there lies an affinity and a knack — a calling — for education.

But none of these exercises in financial discipline are soul-crushing; none of them mean you don't get to live a meaningful, joyful life. Much of the latest psychological research confirms what wise people have known for millennia: joy and meaning are inside jobs .

And while I won't necessarily delight in my children becoming teacher-writers, I do pray that teaching remains a job where you can pursue other things, too — hobbies, families. The pursuit of avocations — even hard ones — can make us better teachers.

I guess my point is that, even though I believe the teaching profession in the USA is presently in dark times for too many teachers, I swear that there's light on the horizon. The insanity simply cannot last; parents will not sit idly by as the quality of their children's education crumbles amidst teacher shortages and testing gluts; educators will continue arguing through their excellence in the classrooms and their voices on the Internet and their advocacy in the public square.
